title: Elbow, Forearm, Wrist & Hand
summary: Covers the bones, joints, ligaments and motions of the elbow, forearm, wrist and hand, with origin/insertion/action/innervation charts for the muscles that move them. Also covers hand arches, creases, grasps and prehension patterns, the median/ulnar/radial nerves, and common elbow, wrist and hand pathologies OT practitioners treat.

exam2: Format: multiple choice, multiple answer, short answer
Short answer: list 5 muscles, their movements, how you used them during the test, how to stretch them
Application: activities and the muscles/joint movements they use
Corresponding glenohumeral and scapular (shoulder girdle) movements
Identify muscles from a scenario, picture, innervation, or origin/insertion
Contraction types (eccentric, concentric, isometric) and which muscle is responsible
Prime motions of muscles (prime mover charts)
Joint types and movements of specific joints
Carpal movements with wrist flexion and extension

sections.heading: Elbow & Radioulnar Joints: Bones, Landmarks, Ligaments, Motion
body: The elbow is built from three bones: the humerus, ulna and radius. Like the knee, it is a hinge joint.

JointBonesLigamentsMotion / ROMType
Elbow (humeroulnar/humeroradial)Humerus, ulna, radiusUlnar (medial) collateral, radial (lateral) collateral; annularFlexion/extension, 0-150°Synovial, uniaxial, hinge
Proximal radioulnarRadius and ulnaAnnular ligament; interosseous membrane (shared with distal RU joint)Supination 0-80°, pronation 0-80°Synovial, uniaxial, pivot
Collateral ligaments (both triangular) give the elbow side-to-side stability. Note: the ulnar collateral ligament is on the medial side and the radial collateral ligament is on the lateral side.
Annular ligament: a ring that wraps the radial head and holds it against the ulna; it sits just below the lateral collateral ligament.
Interosseous membrane: keeps the radius and ulna from separating and adds surface area for muscle attachment.
During pronation/supination the radius rotates around the ulna; the ulna stays put because of its bony shape proximally.

There is no true active hyperextension at the elbow: the olecranon process of the ulna locks into the olecranon fossa of the humerus. If a client hyperextends, suspect ligament laxity rather than bone.

• Trochlea – medial distal humerus; articulates with the ulna.
  • Capitulum – lateral distal humerus, beside the trochlea; articulates with the radial head.
  • Olecranon process – posterior proximal ulna, the point of the elbow; triceps attachment.
  • Medial epicondyle – common flexor tendon origin. Lateral epicondyle – common extensor tendon origin.

Carrying angle: normally 5-15° of valgus, usually larger in females. It exists because the medial distal humerus (trochlea) sits lower than the lateral side (capitulum). It lets the hand come to the mouth (not the shoulder) when the elbow bends.
Functional ROM: most ADLs need only about 30-130° of elbow motion, which is considered WFL (within functional limits).

MotionEnd feelWhy
Elbow flexionSoftMuscle bulk and soft tissue meet
Elbow extensionHard/bonyOlecranon contacts the olecranon fossa
SupinationFirmStretch of ligaments/membrane between radius and ulna
PronationHard/bonyRadius crosses over the ulna

Stability vs mobility: the elbow is far more stable and less mobile than the shoulder. It is most stable for weight bearing in full extension and can handle forces of 1-3x body weight. Elbow flexors are stronger than extensors; both are strongest in midrange.

sections.heading: Muscles of the Elbow & Forearm
body: Prime movers: Flexion – brachialis (the "workhorse"), biceps brachii, brachioradialis. Extension – triceps, anconeus. Supination – biceps brachii, supinator. Pronation – pronator teres (proximal), pronator quadratus (distal).

MuscleOriginInsertionAction (prime)Innervation
Biceps brachiiLong head: supraglenoid tubercle; short head: coracoid processRadial tuberosityElbow flexion, forearm supination (assists shoulder flexion)Musculocutaneous (C5-6)
BrachialisDistal anterior humerusCoronoid process / ulnar tuberosityElbow flexion (any forearm position)Musculocutaneous (C5-6)
BrachioradialisLateral supracondylar ridge of humerusRadial styloid processElbow flexion (strongest in midposition)Radial (C5-6)
Triceps brachiiLong head: infraglenoid tubercle; lateral & medial heads: posterior humerusOlecranon processElbow extension (long head assists shoulder extension)Radial (C6-8)
AnconeusLateral epicondyleOlecranon / posterior proximal ulnaElbow extensionRadial (C7-8)
SupinatorLateral epicondyle and supinator crest of ulnaProximal lateral radiusSupinationRadial (C5-6)
Pronator teresMedial epicondyle and coronoid processMid lateral radiusPronation (assists elbow flexion)Median (C6-7)
Pronator quadratusDistal anterior ulnaDistal anterior radiusPronationMedian (C8-T1)
Several muscles share each action, so some motion is preserved if one nerve is injured. The big exception is elbow extension: triceps and anconeus are both radial nerve.
Palpation tip: resist elbow flexion in midposition and the brachioradialis pops up on top of the forearm.
Supinator is key for turning a doorknob or a screwdriver.

sections.heading: Elbow Pathologies
body: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve entrapment): second most common UE nerve compression after carpal tunnel. The cubital tunnel is on the medial elbow, behind the medial epicondyle. Causes: pressure on the medial elbow, sustained extreme elbow flexion, repetitive motion. S/S: tingling/numbness in ring and small fingers (often worse at night), medial elbow pain, weak grip, poor coordination, atrophy. Treatment: education, rest, avoid full elbow flexion, padded sleeve, towel splint at night to keep the elbow under 90°, nerve glides; surgery (ulnar nerve transposition) if conservative care fails.

Distal biceps tendon rupture: tear at the radial tuberosity insertion, usually muscular males 35-60 lifting with forceful elbow extension. S/S: bruising, swelling, pain, a bulge/gap near the elbow, weak elbow flexion and supination. Post-surgery: cast ~2 weeks, hinged brace (about 40° ext to 70-90° flexion) weeks 2-8, PROM for flexion/supination, gentle strengthening after 8 weeks; full healing 3-6 months.

Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow): overuse of the common extensor tendon, mainly extensor carpi radialis brevis. Ages 30-50, more often men. Pain at the lateral epicondyle that worsens with gripping or lifting in pronation; pain with resisted wrist extension (Cozen's test); weak grip. Treatment: rest, ergonomics, enlarged handles, pacing, avoid combined wrist and elbow extension, ice/heat, stretching, counterforce strap, friction massage; strengthen only once pain resolves.
Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow): overuse of the common flexor tendon; tender at the medial epicondyle with pain on resisted wrist flexion. Treated like tennis elbow.
Little League elbow: repetitive throwing in young athletes puts valgus stress on the elbow, stressing the medial epicondyle tendons.
Nursemaid's (pulled) elbow: children under 5; a sudden pull on the arm makes the radial head slip out from under the annular ligament.

Elbow dislocation: ulna slides off the humerus from high force with the elbow flexed. Supracondylar fracture: break just above the humeral condyles, often a FOOSH in children. Both can injure the brachial artery and lead to Volkmann's ischemic contracture (forearm muscle necrosis from lost blood supply).

sections.heading: Wrist Joints, Ligaments & Carpal Motion
body: Carpals, proximal row lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. Mnemonic: "Steve Left The Party To Take Carol Home."

JointBonesLigamentsMotionsType
RadiocarpalDistal radius + articular disk with scaphoid, lunate, triquetrumPalmar & dorsal radiocarpal; radial & ulnar collateral; joint capsuleFlexion ~80°, extension ~70°, radial dev ~20°, ulnar dev ~30-35°, circumductionEllipsoid (condyloid), biaxial
Intercarpal / MidcarpalCarpal to carpal (inter = within a row; mid = proximal row to distal row)Many small intercarpal ligamentsGlidingGliding, nonaxial

The ulna does not articulate with the carpals. An articular (ulnocarpal) disk fills the gap left because the ulnar styloid is shorter than the radial styloid; it acts as a shock absorber and contacts the lunate and triquetrum. So there is no ulnocarpal joint.
Palmar radiocarpal ligament limits extension and is the stronger one (the functional wrist position is extension). Dorsal radiocarpal ligament limits flexion.
There is no rotation at the wrist; rotation comes from the forearm. Flexion, extension, and radial/ulnar deviation combined make circumduction.

Carpal glide rule: the proximal row glides opposite the hand; the distal row follows the hand. Wrist flexion: proximal row glides dorsally, distal row palmarly. Wrist extension: proximal row glides palmarly, distal row dorsally.
End feels: radial deviation is hard/bony (scaphoid meets radial styloid); all other wrist motions are firm (ligament and capsule tension).

sections.heading: Muscles of the Wrist
body: Wrist-only muscles are the most superficial forearm layer. Anterior (FCR, FCU, palmaris longus) arise from the medial epicondyle; posterior (ECRL, ECRB, ECU) arise from the lateral epicondyle region. All insert on metacarpals except palmaris longus and part of FCU.
Anterior layering: 3 flexor layers (the superficial wrist muscles, then 2 deeper layers mainly for the fingers). Posterior: 1 extensor layer; EDC sits in it but mainly moves the fingers.
Medial-to-lateral superficial flexor order: FCU, PL, FCR, pronator teres. Place your opposite palm on the medial epicondyle: your fingers map those four muscles.

MuscleOriginInsertionAction (prime)Innervation
Flexor carpi radialis (FCR)Medial epicondyle (CFT)Base of 2nd (and 3rd) metacarpalWrist flexion, radial deviationMedian (C6-7)
Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU)Medial epicondyle (CFT) and ulnaPisiform, hook of hamate, base of 5th metacarpalWrist flexion, ulnar deviationUlnar (C8-T1)
Palmaris longus (PL)Medial epicondyle (CFT)Flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosisWrist flexionMedian (C7-8)
Extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL)Lateral supracondylar ridgeBase of 2nd metacarpalWrist extension, radial deviationRadial (C6-7)
Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)Lateral epicondyle (CET)Base of 3rd metacarpalWrist extension (lesser radial deviation)Radial (C6-7)
Extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)Lateral epicondyle (CET)Base of 5th metacarpalWrist extension, ulnar deviationRadial (C6-8)
Palmaris longus is absent in roughly 10% of people, a normal variant. ECRL is the more lateral of the two radial extensors.
Because these muscles cross the elbow, the wrist flexors can weakly assist elbow flexion.

sections.heading: Hand Terminology, Joints & Ligaments
body: Palmar/volar = palm side; dorsal = back; radial = thumb side; ulnar = little finger side. Digits: D1 thumb, D2 index, D3 middle, D4 ring, D5 little.
Thenar = thumb side of the palm; hypothenar = little-finger side. Muscle name clues: pollicis = thumb, indicis = index, minimi = little finger, digitorum = digits 2-5.

JointBonesMotionsType
CMCCarpals + metacarpalsThumb: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, opposition, reposition (+ accessory rotation). D2-3 nearly immobile; D4-5 slight motion for cupping (D5 > D4)Thumb: saddle. D2-D5: gliding
MCPMetacarpals + proximal phalangesFlexion, extension, hyperextension, abduction, adductionEllipsoid (condyloid), biaxial
PIPProximal + middle phalangesFlexion, extensionHinge, uniaxial
DIPMiddle + distal phalangesFlexion, extensionHinge, uniaxial

Wrist/palm ligaments: flexor retinaculum (holds flexor tendons at the wrist, prevents bowstringing); palmar carpal ligament; transverse carpal ligament (roof of the carpal tunnel: 9 flexor tendons + median nerve); extensor retinaculum (dorsal wrist).

Digit ligaments: collateral ligaments on each side of the finger joints prevent side-to-side bending; annular and cruciate pulleys keep flexor tendons close to the bones; the volar plate limits hyperextension.

Extensor hood (extensor expansion): the extensor digitorum tendon spreads over the proximal phalanx and is joined by the lumbricals and interossei, letting these small intrinsics help extend the PIP and DIP.
Skin: palmar skin is thick, immobile and hairless for grip; dorsal skin is thin, supple and mobile so the fist can close.

sections.heading: Extrinsic & Intrinsic Hand Muscles
body: Extrinsic muscles originate outside the hand (forearm/humerus) and insert in the hand. Intrinsic muscles start and end within the hand. The common extensor tendon (CET) comes off the lateral epicondyle; the common flexor tendon (CFT) comes off the medial epicondyle.

Extrinsic muscleOriginInsertionAction (prime)Innervation
Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS)Medial epicondyle, coronoid, anterior radiusSides of middle phalanges D2-5Flex PIP (and MCP, wrist)Median (C7-T1)
Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP)Anterior ulna, interosseous membraneBases of distal phalanges D2-5Flex DIP (the only DIP flexor), PIP, MCP, wristMedian (D2-3) and ulnar (D4-5) (C8-T1)
Flexor pollicis longus (FPL)Anterior radius, interosseous membraneBase of distal phalanx of thumbThumb IP (and MCP) flexionMedian (C8-T1)
Abductor pollicis longus (APL)Posterior radius & ulna, interosseous membraneBase of 1st metacarpalThumb abduction/extension at CMCRadial (C6-7)
Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)Posterior radius, interosseous membraneBase of proximal phalanx of thumbThumb MCP extensionRadial (C6-7)
Extensor pollicis longus (EPL)Posterior ulna, interosseous membraneBase of distal phalanx of thumbThumb IP (and MCP) extensionRadial (C6-8)
Extensor digitorum (ED)Lateral epicondyle (CET)Extensor hood to middle & distal phalanges D2-5Extend MCP, PIP, DIP D2-5 (assists wrist ext)Radial (C6-8)
Extensor indicis (EI)Posterior distal ulnaExtensor hood of D2Extend index fingerRadial (C6-8)
Extensor digiti minimi (EDM)Lateral epicondyle (CET)Extensor hood of D5Extend MCP, PIP, DIP of D5Radial (C6-8)
Anatomical snuffbox (radial dorsal wrist, seen when the thumb extends): EPL is the medial (ulnar) border; APL and EPB form the lateral (radial) border. The scaphoid lies in its floor.

Intrinsic groups: Thenar – OAF (opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis). Hypothenar – OAF (opponens, abductor and flexor digiti minimi). Deep palm – AIL (adductor pollicis, interossei, lumbricals). Dorsal interossei are the only intrinsics on the back of the hand.

Mnemonics: DAB = Dorsal ABduct; PAD = Palmar ADduct. Finger abduction/adduction is measured from the middle finger (D3).

sections.heading: Hand Position, Arches, Creases, Grasps & Prehension
body: Functional position: wrist slightly extended, MCPs and PIPs slightly flexed, thumb in opposition (ready to grasp).

Safe position (intrinsic plus): wrist extended about 20-40°, MCPs flexed about 30-70°, IPs fully extended, thumb in about 45° palmar abduction. Collateral ligaments stay elongated, preventing contracture and claw deformity; used in resting hand orthoses for burns, fractures, arthritis and trauma.

Three arches let the hand cup:
  • Proximal transverse (carpal) arch – formed by the distal row of carpals; fixed.
  • Distal transverse (metacarpal) arch – across the metacarpal heads; mobile, deepens as fingers flex.
  • Longitudinal arch – runs lengthwise from the wrist through each finger ray.

Creases: proximal and distal carpal (wrist) creases; thenar eminence crease (around the thumb base); proximal and distal palmar creases (the distal one roughly marks the MCP joints – splints should end proximal to it to allow MCP flexion); and the digital creases at the MCP (proximal), PIP (middle) and DIP (distal).

Power grips (whole hand, force):
  • Cylindrical – fingers wrap around a cylinder (hammer, glass).
  • Spherical – fingers spread around a ball or doorknob.
  • Hook – fingers flexed at PIP/DIP, thumb not needed (carrying a bag or briefcase).
  • Composite/fist – full finger flexion with thumb wrapped over.
  • Intrinsic plus – MCPs flexed, IPs extended, as when holding a flat object like a book.

Precision grips (fine control):
  • Tip pinch (2-point) – tip of thumb to tip of index (picking up a pin or coin).
  • Three-jaw chuck (tripod) – thumb pad against index and middle pads (holding a pen).
  • Lateral (key) pinch – thumb pad to the side of the index finger (turning a key).
  • Lumbrical grip – MCPs flexed, PIPs/DIPs extended, thumb opposing (holding a dinner plate).

sections.heading: Nerves of the Upper Extremity
body: UE nerves come from roughly C5-T1 (the course notes say C1-T1; the brachial plexus itself is C5-T1) and merge in the brachial plexus. The radial nerve comes from the posterior cord, the ulnar from the medial cord, and the median from both lateral and medial cords. Arteries supply muscles; veins remove waste.

NerveKey musclesSensory areaInjury sign
RadialTriceps, anconeus, brachioradialis, supinator, all wrist & finger extensors, APL, EPB, EPLDorsum of hand on radial side (thumb, index, middle, half ring), except fingertipsWrist drop – cannot extend wrist/fingers; often from humeral shaft fracture or "Saturday night palsy"
MedianPronators, FCR, PL, FDS, lateral FDP, FPL, thenar OAF, lumbricals 1-2Palmar thumb, index, middle and radial half of ring fingerApe hand/loss of opposition, thenar atrophy; carpal tunnel syndrome
UlnarFCU, medial FDP, hypothenar OAF, adductor pollicis, interossei, lumbricals 3-4, deep FPBLittle finger and ulnar half of ring finger (palmar & dorsal)Claw hand (D4-5), weak grip/pinch; cubital tunnel syndrome
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-6) supplies biceps and brachialis, so elbow flexion can partly survive a radial nerve injury, but elbow extension cannot.

sections.heading: Wrist & Hand Pathologies
body: Colles fracture: distal radius fracture from FOOSH with dorsal (posterior) displacement of the distal fragment and radial shortening; the classic "dinner fork" deformity.
Smith's fracture: the reverse of Colles; from a fall on the back of the hand, with palmar (volar) displacement.

Scaphoid fracture: the most commonly fractured carpal, often from FOOSH with wrist hyperextension and radial deviation. Poor blood supply means slow healing and risk of avascular necrosis. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is a red flag.
Complications after wrist fracture that OT addresses: edema, scar tissue, nerve compression, and lingering wrist and finger stiffness.
Ganglion cyst: benign fluid-filled mass, most often on the dorsal wrist.

Carpal tunnel syndrome: median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel (under the transverse carpal ligament with 9 flexor tendons). Tingling, pain and weakness in the palmar thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger.
De Quervain's tenosynovitis: thickened sheath of APL and EPB on the radial wrist. Finkelstein test: fist with the thumb tucked in, then ulnarly deviate the wrist.
Swan neck deformity: MCP flexion, PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion; often with RA.
Boutonniere deformity: MCP extension, PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension; often with RA or a central slip injury.
Ulnar drift: fingers deviate ulnarly at the MCPs; common in RA.
Mallet finger: the DIP stays flexed and cannot actively extend (terminal extensor tendon injury, e.g., ball striking the fingertip).
Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis): a swollen tendon sheath or tendon nodule catches in the A1 pulley so the finger locks or snaps.
Dupuytren's contracture: nodular thickening of the palmar aponeurosis that pulls fingers (usually ring and small) into flexion.
Tendinitis: tendon inflammation from microtears due to overuse or repetitive strain.
Skier's thumb / gamekeeper's thumb: injury to the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP; skier's is an acute tear, gamekeeper's is a chronic stretching injury.
Osteoarthritis: commonly affects the thumb CMC (base-of-thumb pain with pinch) and the DIP/PIP joints of the fingers.

sections.heading: Functional & Clinical Application
body: Placing a plate in an overhead cabinet: elbow extension, forearm pronation. Bringing soup to the mouth: elbow flexion, forearm supination. Reaching for a desk phone: extension + pronation; holding it to the ear: flexion + supination.
Overhead triceps stretch (arm up, other hand pushes the hand down behind the head): right elbow goes into flexion, stretching the triceps.
Forearms flat on a table, pressing down: no joint motion, so it is an isometric contraction, strengthening the triceps and pronators.

Lowering a weight from the shoulder to anatomical position: elbow extension with an eccentric contraction of the elbow flexors (biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis); an open-chain movement because the hand is free.
Reverse muscle action: the origin moves toward the insertion, e.g., the elbow flexors pulling the body up in a chin-up, or triceps during a push-up.
To stretch a muscle, move every joint it crosses into the opposite of its prime actions (e.g., stretch FCR with wrist extension + ulnar deviation and elbow extension).

sections.heading: Exam 2 Checklist
body: Format: multiple choice, multiple answer and short answer. One short answer asks you to list 5 muscles, their movements, how you used them during the test, and how to stretch them. Bring your Neuro packet.

Strategy: act out the movements as you read. Think about all motions of a joint when contracting or stretching. Focus on what the question actually asks. Write your prime mover chart down at the start and use it as a reference.

Know:
  • Rotator cuff muscles; shoulder (glenohumeral) vs shoulder girdle (scapula) paired motions; scapulohumeral rhythm; bursa (from the shoulder unit)
  • Prime motions of every muscle; identifying a muscle from a scenario, picture, origin/insertion or innervation
  • Contraction types (concentric, eccentric, isometric) and which muscle is working
  • Reverse muscle actions
  • Bones in each joint, joint types, joint motions and ROM norms
  • Motions that stretch a muscle
  • Pathologies/conditions
  • Carpal glides with wrist flexion/extension; carrying angle
  • Ligaments in the digits; extensor hood; anatomical snuffbox
  • Thenar vs hypothenar; arches and creases; grasps and grips
  • Median, ulnar and radial innervation

questions.q: Which joint allows forearm pronation and supination?
questions.explain: The pivot-type proximal (and distal) radioulnar joints produce forearm rotation.

questions.q: During pronation, what does the radius do?
choices: Stays fixed while the ulna rotates
questions.explain: The radius moves around the ulna, which is held in place by its bony shape.

questions.q: What type of joint is the elbow (humeroulnar) joint?
questions.explain: The elbow flexes and extends in one plane like a hinge.

questions.q: Which ligament encircles the radial head?
questions.explain: The annular ligament wraps the radial head and holds it to the ulna.

questions.q: What structure blocks elbow hyperextension?
choices: The coronoid process in the radial fossa
The olecranon process fitting into the olecranon fossa
questions.explain: Bone-on-bone contact of olecranon and fossa gives the hard end feel.

questions.q: What is the normal elbow carrying angle?
questions.explain: A 5-15 degree valgus angle is normal and usually larger in females.

questions.q: Most ADLs require roughly how much elbow range?
questions.explain: Functional elbow range is about 30-130 degrees.

questions.q: Which landmark articulates with the radial head?
questions.explain: The lateral capitulum meets the radius; the trochlea meets the ulna.

questions.q: Which muscle is the elbow flexion 'workhorse'?
questions.explain: Brachialis flexes the elbow in every forearm position.

questions.q: Which muscles are prime movers for supination?
questions.explain: Biceps and supinator turn the palm up.

questions.q: Which muscles are prime movers for pronation?
questions.explain: Both pronators are median-nerve muscles.

questions.q: All of these flex the elbow EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Anconeus assists the triceps in elbow extension.

questions.q: Which elbow flexor is innervated by the radial nerve?
questions.explain: Biceps and brachialis are musculocutaneous; brachioradialis is radial.

questions.q: Which muscle is most important for turning a doorknob to open it (palm-up rotation)?
questions.explain: Supination turns the knob and screwdriver.

questions.q: A radial nerve injury in the arm would most likely eliminate which elbow motion?
questions.explain: Triceps and anconeus are both radial, so no backup exists for extension.

questions.q: A client reports tingling in the ring and small fingers that worsens when sleeping with elbows bent. Which condition fits?
questions.explain: Ulnar nerve compression at the medial elbow is aggravated by sustained flexion.

questions.q: Which night positioning is recommended for cubital tunnel syndrome?
choices: A towel splint keeping the elbow under 90 degrees of flexion
questions.explain: Limiting flexion reduces ulnar nerve stretch and pressure.

questions.q: Which muscle is mainly involved in lateral epicondylitis?
questions.explain: ECRB from the common extensor tendon is the usual culprit in tennis elbow.

questions.q: Pain with resisted wrist flexion and tenderness at the medial epicondyle suggests:
questions.explain: Golfer's elbow involves the common flexor tendon.

questions.q: A distal biceps tendon rupture causes weakness in which motions?
questions.explain: Biceps flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm.

questions.q: A 3-year-old cries and won't use the arm after being lifted by the hand. The most likely injury is:
questions.explain: A sudden pull slips the radial head out of the annular ligament.

questions.q: Which recommendation fits a client with tennis elbow?
choices: Use enlarged handles and avoid combined wrist and elbow extension
Keep the elbow in sustained full flexion
Increase repetitive hammering to toughen the tendon
questions.explain: Rest, ergonomics and adaptive tools come first; strengthen only after pain resolves.

questions.q: Which bones articulate with the distal radius at the radiocarpal joint?
questions.explain: The radius and disk meet the proximal carpals except the pisiform.

questions.q: What type of joint is the radiocarpal joint?
questions.explain: It allows flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation.

questions.q: Which motion is NOT available at the wrist?
questions.explain: Rotation comes from the forearm, not the wrist.

questions.q: During wrist flexion, the proximal row of carpals glides:
questions.explain: The proximal row moves opposite the hand.

questions.q: During wrist flexion, the distal row of carpals glides:
questions.explain: The distal row follows the hand.

questions.q: During wrist extension, the proximal row of carpals glides:
questions.explain: The proximal row glides opposite the hand's dorsal motion.

questions.q: Which wrist motion has a hard/bony end feel?
questions.explain: The scaphoid meets the radial styloid; other motions are firm.

questions.q: Which muscle flexes the wrist and radially deviates it?
questions.explain: FCR runs to the 2nd metacarpal on the radial side.

questions.q: Which muscle extends the wrist and ulnarly deviates it?
questions.explain: ECU inserts on the 5th metacarpal.

questions.q: Which wrist flexor inserts on the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis?
questions.explain: PL is the only wrist flexor without a metacarpal insertion.

questions.q: Which muscle extends the wrist with only a lesser role in radial deviation?
questions.explain: ECRB inserts centrally on the 3rd metacarpal.

questions.q: Where do the wrist extensors mainly originate?
questions.explain: The CET arises from the lateral epicondyle region.

questions.q: Which distal radius fracture shows dorsal displacement and a dinner fork deformity?
questions.explain: Colles results from FOOSH with posterior displacement.

questions.q: Why can a scaphoid fracture heal slowly?
questions.explain: Poor vascular supply risks avascular necrosis.

questions.q: What passes through the carpal tunnel?
choices: Nine flexor tendons and the median nerve
questions.explain: FDS (4), FDP (4) and FPL plus the median nerve.

questions.q: Pollicis, minimi and digitorum refer to:
questions.explain: These are standard muscle-name terms.

questions.q: Thenar refers to the:
questions.explain: Hypothenar is the little-finger side.

questions.q: What prevents the finger joints from bending side to side?
questions.explain: Collaterals on each side stabilize the joint.

questions.q: What is the main job of the extensor hood?
choices: Help small intrinsic muscles extend the PIPs and DIPs
questions.explain: Lumbricals and interossei join the hood to extend the IPs.

questions.q: Which joint is ellipsoid and biaxial in the fingers?
questions.explain: MCPs flex/extend and abduct/adduct.

questions.q: Which tendons form the anatomical snuffbox borders?
choices: EPL medially; APL and EPB laterally
questions.explain: The scaphoid lies in the snuffbox floor.

questions.q: Which muscle is the only one that flexes the DIP joints?
questions.explain: FDP inserts on the distal phalanges.

questions.q: The thenar intrinsic group (OAF) includes:
choices: Opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis
questions.explain: Thenar OAF muscles move the thumb.

questions.q: Which muscles abduct the fingers?
questions.explain: DAB: Dorsal ABduct.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies most thumb thenar muscles?
questions.explain: The median nerve supplies thenar OAF.

questions.q: What defines an intrinsic hand muscle?
choices: It originates and inserts within the hand
questions.explain: Extrinsics start outside the hand.

questions.q: What are the three arches of the hand?
choices: Proximal transverse, distal transverse, and longitudinal
questions.explain: These arches let the hand cup.

questions.q: Which arch is mobile and deepens with finger flexion?
questions.explain: The metacarpal-head arch is the mobile one.

questions.q: Holding a key between the thumb pad and the side of the index finger is a:
questions.explain: Lateral pinch uses the side of the index.

questions.q: Holding a pen with the thumb, index and middle fingers is a:
questions.explain: Thumb pad opposes index and middle pads.

questions.q: Holding a dinner plate with MCPs flexed and IPs straight is a:
questions.explain: MCP flexion with IP extension is the lumbrical action.

questions.q: Grasping a doorknob or ball with spread fingers is a:
questions.explain: The fingers curve around a round object.

questions.q: Difficulty with thumb opposition and numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers point to injury of the:
questions.explain: The median nerve supplies thenar muscles and that sensory area.

questions.q: Which nerve injury causes wrist drop?
questions.explain: The radial nerve supplies all wrist and finger extensors.

questions.q: Sensation on the palmar side of the small finger is supplied by the:
questions.explain: Ulnar covers D5 and half of D4.

questions.q: Which describes a swan neck deformity?
choices: MCP extension, PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension
MCP flexion, PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion
questions.explain: Swan neck hyperextends the PIP.

questions.q: Which describes a boutonniere deformity?
choices: MCP extension, PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension
MCP flexion, PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion
Flexion contracture of the ring finger
questions.explain: Boutonniere flexes the PIP.

questions.q: A client cannot straighten the tip of the finger after a ball struck it. This is:
questions.explain: The terminal extensor tendon is injured at the DIP.

questions.q: Dupuytren's contracture involves thickening of the:
choices: Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb
questions.explain: Nodules in the palmar fascia pull fingers into flexion.

questions.q: Ulnar drift of the fingers at the MCPs is most associated with:
questions.explain: RA weakens MCP supporting structures.

questions.q: Placing a dinner plate in an overhead cabinet uses elbow ____ and forearm ____.
questions.explain: Reaching up with palm down is extension plus pronation.

questions.q: Bringing a spoonful of soup to the mouth uses elbow ____ and forearm ____.
questions.explain: The hand comes to the mouth palm up.

questions.q: Slowly lowering a dumbbell from the shoulder to the side involves which contraction of the elbow flexors?
questions.explain: The flexors lengthen to control the descent.

questions.q: Pressing the forearms down into a table without moving is what contraction type?
questions.explain: No joint motion occurs while the triceps and pronators work.

questions.q: When a muscle's origin moves toward its insertion, as in a push-up, it is called:
questions.explain: The distal segment is fixed and the proximal part moves.

questions.q: The overhead triceps stretch puts the stretched elbow into:
questions.explain: Elbow flexion elongates the triceps.

questions.q: To stretch the flexor carpi radialis, position the wrist in:
questions.explain: Stretch by moving opposite every prime action.

questions.q: On Exam 2, the short-answer item asks you to list how many muscles with their movements and stretches?
questions.explain: The rundown asks for 5 muscles, their movements, use during the test and stretches.
